customers by lower-cased e-mail, keeps the oldest record of each group,
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: Drop or qualify the premise. The design's Context states that "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address": with the planned rule, the job fuses those buyers into the oldest record, reassigns every buyer's orders to it and deletes the other buyers' records and billing addresses. Choose a key that tells distinct people apart (e-mail plus name and/or billing address, or exclude shared mailboxes), state it in the spec's requirement, and add a scenario where two different buyers share one e-mail and stay separate.
findings.title: The merge key rests on an assumption the design's own context contradicts

findings.evidence: moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The merge is a one-way door: once the duplicate rows are deleted and their orders moved, nothing in the plan records which order belonged to which record, nor keeps the deleted name and billing address. Add a way back — keep a merge log (merged id → surviving id, the deleted row's data) or soft-delete, and a dry-run or staged first run — plus a task that checks it.
findings.title: Records are deleted with no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: The two scenarios ("Two records, one e-mail", "No duplicate") leave unspecified what the design already decides or the data allows: e-mails that differ only by case (the design lower-cases, the requirement does not say so), duplicates whose name or billing address differ (which values the surviving record keeps), and a guest checkout that inserts a customer or an order for a record while the job is merging it. Add a scenario per case and extend task 1.1 to test them.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path

findings.recommendation: The change adds "A nightly job" (`jobs/merge_customers.py`) that must be scheduled, run and monitored, and that deletes rows in production; tick `operations` so its expert reviews how the job is deployed, scheduled and watched, or give the reason on the line.
findings.title: The operations domain is unticked for a new scheduled job

findings.evidence: Guest checkouts create a new customer each time; support sees five records for one person.
findings.recommendation: The Why names the cause — `guest_checkout` in `app/checkout.py` inserts a new customer on every order — yet the plan only cleans up after it nightly, so duplicates keep appearing during the day, and the design's "Alternatives considered" weighs only fuzzy matching. Say why reusing an existing customer at checkout was not chosen, or plan it alongside the job.
findings.title: The cause of the duplicates is left in place
